newsitem.title: TUNISIA: British official seeks swift Israeli redeployment.
newsitem.headline: British official seeks swift Israeli redeployment.

text.p: A British minister said on Thursday Israel must carry out its promised withdrawals from Hebron and other parts of the West Bank to restore trust between Israel and the Palestinians.
"We continue to hope that agreement on Hebron will be reached soon. That agreement is vital," British Foreign and Commonwealth Office Minister Jeremy Hanley said in Tunis.

"But if it does come soon we must not be carried away by relief and euphoria. There is still a long way to go before an element of trust is restored between the parties," Hanley added in a speech prepared for the Tunisian-British Chamber of Commerce.
"That can only happen if Hebron is followed swiftly by implementation of other outstanding elements in the Interim Agreement. The most important are further redeployments on the West Bank," he said.

Negotiators say a deal on Israel's overdue handover of 80 percent of Hebron is all but reached. The argument now is on the timing and scope of further redeployments which should be completed by next September 7 under a 1995 interim agreement on implementing the Oslo peace accords.

"The lesson of Hebron has been that there is no alternative to persistence and patience. Pressures have accumulated until in the end it is clear that there is only one way out of Hebron. That way is to proceed according to the blueprint of the Oslo Accords," Hanley added.

Israel's right-wing government wants to delay redeployment in the West Bank until 1999, while Palestinians want to control the promised 90 percent of the West Bank before negotiating sensitive "final status" issues like Jerusalem, refugees and the powers of a Palestinian government.
Hanley said the European Union will become more involved in promoting peace between Israel and the Syrian and Palestinian sides, a process that needs more attention.
"We have been reminded of that by the recent appalling bombing of a bus in Damascus. I extend my deepest condolences to the government in Damascus," he said.

"This and the recent outrage in the Hebron market remind us that there are Arab as well as Israeli victims of terrorism and that the absence of security and stability in the region causes suffering on all sides," Hanley said.
A bomb in a bus in Damascus last week killed 11 people and wounded 42. Syria blamed Israel but Israel denied any involvement.
The same week an Israeli reserve soldier opposed to any Israeli withdrawal from Hebron went on a shooting spree, wounding seven Arab shoppers in the market in the West Bank town of 100,000 Arabs.
